segments.narration: Five different civilisations have been credited with carving one boulder. Dighton Rock. Forty tons of sandstone, hauled out of a river in Massachusetts.
A minister sketched its marks in 1680, and that drawing sits in the British Museum. Cotton Mather wrote the rock up ten years later.
Then the readings began. Phoenician letters, said Ezra Stiles in 1783. Norsemen, said a Danish scholar in 1837. Chinese sailors, said an author in 2002.
A Brown University professor found a Portuguese name in the scratches: Miguel Corte-Real, 1511. A 2017 book pulled that apart line by line.
No translation has survived scrutiny. The marks look like the Indigenous petroglyphs found across New England, and the mineral crust grown into the carvings means nobody can date them.

verdicts.claim: Ezra Stiles proposed a Phoenician origin in 1783, Carl Christian Rafn a Norse origin in 1837, and Gavin Menzies a Chinese origin in 2002.
verdicts.note: 100% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 3 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Edmund Delabarre of Brown University read the inscription as naming Miguel Corte-Real and the year 1511, and Douglas Hunter debunked that reading in 2017.
verdicts.note: 87% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 2 number(s)

verdicts.claim: The Norse and Corte-Real readings have been rejected, Indigenous petroglyphs are found throughout New England, and mineral crusts on the carvings prevent accurate dating.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia records the rejections, notes a schematic face resembling an Indigenous petroglyph in eastern Vermont, and still calls the origin uncertain; ExplorersWeb explains the weathering and mineral-crust problem that blocks dating. The narration therefore says the marks 'look like' Indigenous petroglyphs rather than asserting a proven origin.
